paragraphs.source_en: This book argues for the existence of the pre-Pastoral rock art in the Central Sahara. Archaeological evidence suggests that the low chronology is not sustainable for a region that shows unquestionable signs of artistic production as early as the 10th millennium BP in the form of decorated pottery which will be discussed later. The general archaeological evidence strongly suggests that the complex hunter-gatherer societies, attested in the excavations, produced rock art.

paragraphs.source_en: The high chronology proposed here places the earliest stages of the Bubaline, Kel Essuf and Round Heads at least to the 10th millennium BP and the Pastoral style to the 8th millennium BP. The Bubaline style may have originated much earlier than 10,000 BP. Although this hypothesis has not yet been proved, the Bubaline art can be compared with other African engravings. In the Nile Valley in Egypt one of the major Nilotic rock art assemblages, Qurta, was recently attributed to the Late Palaeolithic (Huyge 2009; Huyge et al. 2011). These engravings almost exclusively represent short-horned wild bovids and only a few wild animals such as hippopotamuses, gazelles and birds are depicted. paragraphs.source_en: Too little is known about the Kel Essuf images but they certainly precede the Round Head images in the relative chronology. Regarding the Round Head paintings, for the moment they cannot be considered earlier than 10,000 BP since we do not possess archaeological data confirming human occupation before this date. These paintings may have originated together with another artistic tradition, the pottery, which is shown to be as early as the 10th millennium BP.
